extracted.intended_audience: readers of Benjamin Franklin's collected letters; Franklin's correspondents (family, friends, and intellectual acquaintances)
extracted.subtask_description: Collected personal letters by Benjamin Franklin giving advice on conduct, business, reading, marriage, and politics; the page models epistolary style and practical counsel for friends and family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to appearances with the vulnerable
rubrics_metrics.description: “appearances should therefore be attended to in our conduct towards them as well as relatives.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with people in delicate circumstances who may be apt to suspect, avoid adding causes for suspicion; be mindful of appearances and behave considerately to preserve their peace of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain correspondence while traveling
rubrics_metrics.description: Franklin requests sporadic letters while abroad and gives clear directions for where to leave mail (e.g., Pennsylvania Coffee-house, Birchin Lane, London).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep occasional contact when journeying; provide precise mail directions or addresses to ensure correspondence continues during long stays away.

rubrics_metrics.name: A trade requires industry to be valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: “A trade is a valuable thing; but unless a habit of industry be acquired with it, it turns out of little use.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training in a craft is only useful if accompanied by a habit of steady, industrious work; employers and apprentices should cultivate industry, not rely on the mere possession of a trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry, frugality, and prudence in a spouse equal fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: “Industry, frugality, and prudent economy in a wife, are to a tradesman, in their effects, a fortune; and a fortune sufficient for Benjamin, if his expectations are reasonable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a marriage partner (especially for a tradesman), value practical virtues (industry, frugality, economy) as equivalent to or more important than monetary dowries; these habits can create prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid counterfeit or deceptive branding
rubrics_metrics.description: Franklin advises: do not put the Franklin arms on soap; 'the other would look too much like an attempt to counterfeit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truthful branding and marks. If you apprenticed with an original maker, you may note that experience in ads but should use your own device/mark on products; avoid appropriating another's arms or marks which would appear fraudulent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only vend genuinely good products
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let a box be sent to her (but not unless it be right good), and she will immediately return the ready money for it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before sending goods to agents or sellers, ensure the product quality is high; doing otherwise harms reputation and sales. Use trusted intermediaries only for genuinely good wares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty is essential in trades liable to suspicion (goldsmiths example)
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is one accomplishment without which he cannot possibly thrive in that trade (i. e., to be perfectly honest). It is a business that, though ever so uprightly managed, is always liable to suspicion...if a man is once detected in the smallest fraud it soon becomes public...so at once he is ruined.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In trades where trust is central (e.g., goldsmithing), maintain impeccable honesty and faithful workmanship; even a small fraud destroys reputation and future business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not displace competent officers for favoritism
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a rule with me not to remove any officer that behaves well, keeps regular accounts, and pays duly; and I think the rule is founded on reason and justice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments and removals should be governed by merit and regularity of conduct, not by personal favors or resentments; avoid using influence to gratify inclinations at the expense of fair practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reconciliation; avoid family quarrels
rubrics_metrics.description: “Above all things, I dislike family quarrels...I wish you were reconciled, and that I will love that side best that is most ready to forgive and oblige the other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When hearing only one side of a domestic dispute, refrain from judgment; encourage forgiveness and reconciliation rather than taking or inflaming sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read accessible works to instruct beginners
rubrics_metrics.description: Books are 'written in the familiar, easy manner for which the French are so remarkable; and afford a good deal of philosophic and practical knowledge, unembarassed with the dry mathematics used by more exact reasoners, but which is apt to discourage young beginners.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For novices, choose texts that explain principles in an accessible, practical manner rather than overly mathematical treatises which may discourage learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read actively: take notes and consult a dictionary
rubrics_metrics.description: “I would advise you to read with a pen in your hand, and enter in a little book short hints...have a good dictionary at hand, to consult immediately when you meet with a word you do not comprehend the precise meaning of.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying, take concise notes of curious or useful points to aid memory and future use. Use a dictionary immediately to learn unfamiliar terms; this effort diminishes over time and improves comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hesitate to ask mentors questions
rubrics_metrics.description: “When any point occurs in which you would be glad to have farther information than your book affords you, I beg you would not in the least apprehend that I should think it a trouble to receive and answer your questions. It will be a pleasure, and no trouble.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learners should feel free to ask knowledgeable friends or mentors for clarification; experienced correspondents welcome genuine inquiries and can direct to further resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of early marriage and forming habits young
rubrics_metrics.description: Franklin argues early marriages 'stand the best chance of happiness...The temper and habits of the young are not yet become so stiff and uncomplying...By early marriage we are blessed with more children...our children are therefore educated and settled in the world by noon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General counsel: early marriage often promotes mutual adaptation, earlier formation of useful habits, more time to enjoy later life, and greater likelihood parents live to see children educated; consider particular circumstances nevertheless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat spouse with respect; avoid joking slights
rubrics_metrics.description: “Treat your wife always with respect;...Never use a slighting expression to her, even in jest; for slights in jest, after frequent bandyings, are apt to end in angry earnest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent respect in marital conduct, avoiding even joking insults, because repeated small slights can accumulate into genuine hostility. Respect begets respect from others as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal virtues lead to success: industry, frugality, sobriety, virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: “Be studious in your profession...Be industrious and frugal, and you will be rich. Be sober and temperate, and you will be healthy. Be in general virtuous, and you will be happy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical moral advice linking professional diligence, thrift, temperance, and general virtue to tangible outcomes: wealth, health, and happiness. Encourages steady personal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inquiry and representation, not force, in managing colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Franklin recommends that when discontent exists Parliament send 'two or three of their body into the discontented provinces to inquire into the grievances...that mild measures might be used to remedy what was amiss before any severe steps were taken to enforce obedience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer investigation, representation, and moderate remedies to punitive force when addressing political grievances; using force risks alienation and greater harm to relations and commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary power over colonies should include fair representation for stable union
rubrics_metrics.description: “A consolidating union, by a fair and equal representation of all the parts of this empire in Parliament, is the only firm basis on which its political grandeur and prosperity can be founded.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a durable imperial union, legislative power should be accompanied by real representation of the governed; absence of representation undermines legitimacy and fosters resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal taxes without representation will be objected to
rubrics_metrics.description: Franklin notes: 'internal taxes laid on them by Parliament are still, and ever will be, objected to' because assemblies view them as internal matters requiring local assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should recognize that imposing internal taxes on subordinate legislatures without local consent is likely to provoke persistent objection and political friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure value by the labor needed to produce necessities
rubrics_metrics.description: “Food is always necessary to all...Is not this kind of labour, then, the fittest to be the standard by which to measure the values of all other labour...may not even gold and silver be thus valued?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes an economic criterion: use the amount of labor required to produce essential goods (food) as a standard for valuing other goods and labor; this is an argument for labor/utility-based valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer oxen to horses for agricultural efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Franklin relays the view that 'farmers are more thriving in those parts of the country where horned cattle are used, than in those where the labour is done by horses...The latter are said to require twice the quantity of land to maintain them and, after all, are not good to eat.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For agricultural policy or farm management, consider draught animals' maintenance costs and food value: oxen may be more land- and resource-efficient than horses in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When sending gifts of books, choose works appropriate to recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: Franklin sends books 'written in the familiar, easy manner...and afford a good deal of philosophic and practical knowledge' as a 'small mark of my esteem and friendship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select instructional or pleasurable texts suited to the recipient's level and tastes when sending books as tokens; explain their usefulness and encourage active engagement.
